Sabadia Parole

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The story of wife killer Dr Omar Sabadia who has been placed on parole after serving 20 years of a 50 year sentence.

Unique Selling Point:
For the first time on television, the children of Zahida Sabadia talk about growing up without their parents, after their father hired three hitmen to kill their mother.

Summary:
Why did the parole Board place Dr Sabadia on parole, without informing the family of the parole hearing. Will their voices be heard? Former Chairman of the Parole Review Board explains what happens now. Dr Sabadia's lawyer explains why his client is long overdue for parole consideration, after serving less than half his sentence.

Press Release:


Parole Board Bungle
Omar Sabadia made headlines in 1996 when he murdered his wife, Zahida, a medical student with three small children. The judge sentenced Sabadia to 50 years in prison and ordered that he serve a minimum of 35 years before parole could even be considered. Now after just 20 years in prison and despite his children’s objections, the parole board has granted his application and in just a few weeks, Sabadia will be out on parole. Carte Blanche asks: how did this happen?


Script:


SABADIA PAROLE

V/O: Anjum and Khatija were 8 and 4 when their mother was kidnapped and murdered in a fake hijacking.

Khatija: It was a very, very difficult time because I was 4-years old, and when you’re 4 that’s when you most clingy to your mother.

Anjum: As children we had questions. We didn’t know what happened to our mother. She just disappeared. We didn’t know our father killed her. And we found out later, and to find out that your father did that to his children, like someone who is supposed to love you and care for you and protect you.

V/O: In 1996 Zahida Sabadia was a final year medical student at Medunsa. Her husband Dr Omar Sabadia was a psychiatrist practicing in Pretoria. As a compulsive gambler he had financial problems and so insured Zahida’s life for R3.2m. He then convinced a patient, Patrick Manyape to recruit hitmen to kill his wife. Richard Malema and Albert Moeketsane were promised huge financial rewards, and on Sunday the 11th of February the trap was set.

Sabadia insisted on driving his wife to the Ga-rankuwa Hospital to do ward rounds. On the way home they stopped at Bimbo’s to order food. As they left, the fake hijackers pounced. Zahida was pistol-whipped and bundled into the car. Sabadia then drove to a deserted area not far from the hospital, where he watched Moeketsane taking his wife deeper into the bush. There she was stabbed and strangled before being tied to a tree with a raincoat.

The family hired private investigators to solve the crime, and within three weeks Omar Sabadia had made a confession to the police. He took them back to Garankuwa and pointed out where the body was.

Anjum: I remember my mother’s funeral. We were woken up in the middle of the night and told our mother passed away. I remember sitting there and praying.

V/O: The children grew up in Louis Trichardt with their grandparents and took their surname.

Khatija: As far as I’m concerned, my grandfather is my father. Omar Sabadia will never be my father.

V/O: At Medunsa’s graduation ceremony Anjum accepted Zahida’s degree on behalf of her late mother.

V/O: Omar Sabadia and his three accomplices were all convicted of kidnapping and murder.

Link: Dr Omar Sabadia has been behind bars since 1998. He’s serving a 50-year sentence, but like all prisoners in South Africa, he is entitled to apply for parole.

Julian: Currently it means that you would have to do half of that before you are eligible for parole, but anyone sentenced before 1 October 2004 has to do a third of their sentence.

V/O: Julian Knight is Omar Sabadia’s lawyer. With presidential amnesties and credits earned for good behaviour, his client is long overdue for consideration for parole.

Julian: He would then be eligible for placement at 14 years and 7 months, which is September 2012. We are now June 2018.

V/O: But the parole board wouldn’t consider Sabadia because of the words of the sentencing Judge. The family’s lawyer Ahmed Suliman, was in court that day and remembers it well.

Ahmed: He said if the parole board heeds my recommendations this man should stay in prison for 35 years and he should only come out when he’s 78 years of age.

Link 2: When Judge Eddie Stafford sentenced him in 1998 he recommended that Sabadia be imprisoned for a minimum of 35 years before being considered for parole. But that was just a recommendation. At the time the Judge was not entitled to prescribe how long Sabadia should be detained.

Siraj: The comments of a judge are comments which must be taken into account, but they are not gospel.

V/O: Judge Siraj Desai was the first chairperson of the Parole Review Board.

Siraj: The Correctional Services board takes into account what the judge says, but also exercises the ultimate analysis and independent discretion.

V/O: The High Court has since ordered the Parole Board to disregard the 35-year recommendation. Sabadia had two parole hearings last year, and the family attended both.

Link: Prisons are not a happy place. In fact, most of us want to avoid even a brief visit. But family members who want to be present during a parole hearing will have to come to prison and endure the trauma of facing the perpetrator across a table.

V/O: Anjum is a law graduate, and she and Khatija now run a beauty bar and spa in Pretoria. They insisted on objecting in person at the parole hearings.

Anjum: We were stressed out, we were anxious, we didn’t know what to expect. In fact, I thought we were going to walk into a big courtroom, and when we got there I realized it was a little boardroom and we were going to be so close to him.

Khatija: It was very emotional for me, especially seeing Omar Sabadia after 20 years. You know, I thought I’d go there and he’d at least acknowledge us. He didn’t even look at us.

Julian: He was instructed by the Parole Board not to have any eye contact with them and look forward at the wall, and they then pointed fingers at them and expressed their displeasure at what they had done.

Anjum: He sat down, and I approached him, and I told him he hurt us. And he looked down, and I thought I’d get answers or an apology, and I got nothing. Nothing, and that hurt.

Devi: Anjum what did you want him to say to you?

Anjum: I wanted him to say he’s sorry. Just something, I wanted answers, and I got nothing.

Julian: Incidentally they have had no contact with him during his entire incarceration. At that parole hearing was the first time that he had seen his children since he had been put in jail for the crime that he committed.

V/O: But Sabadia has sent letters through other people to try and communicate with his daughters.

Anjum: He said he doesn’t remember killing my mother because he was bi-polar. The second letter was sent after my meeting with him, and a lady friend of his sent me a letter saying that my anger is going to drive him to commit suicide.

V/O: Omar Sabadia is now 63-years old.

Devi: What’s he like?

Julian: Like a very old prisoner. He’s not very healthy person, he looks a very weak person, from a physical point of view.

V/O: In December the Parole Board postponed the hearing to take further legal advice.

Link: Omar Sabadia’s lawyer felt the Parole Board was taking too long. He came back to the Pretoria High Court to force them to set a new date. On the 20th of March the court ordered them to convene a parole hearing within 30 days.

V/O: On the 12th of April the parole board informed the parties that the hearing was scheduled for the 30th of April. But neither attorney was available that day.

Ahmed: I went back to them immediately and I said to them please can we do this matter on the 10th of May?

V/O: He heard nothing further until the 16th of May.

Ahmed: And the next thing is we get an email, and the email says that a parole board hearing was convened for 20th of April, and he will be granted parole and his date of release is 20th of June.

V/O: But the law gives victim’s families the right to be present at any Parole Board hearing. So why did the Department of Correctional Services go ahead without informing either side of the new date? We asked Regional Commissioner Takane Grace Molatedi.

Grace: Our plan was to see Dr Sabadia on the 30th of April. We then also invited the family. That’s when we received a court order that said we must consider him before the 20th of April.

Devi: Because a court order gives you no choice?

Grace: Yes, we had to comply with the court order.

Devi: So, knowing that the victim’s family weren’t represented you had to comply? The court ruling comes first?

Grace: The court ruling comes first.

Devi: Okay

Siraj: The High Court can compel the hearing to take place, that is within its jurisdiction. But it can’t compel the parole Board not to hear or give effect to the voice of victims. Nobody who has offended seriously will walk on the streets, unless there’s been some input from the families of the victims of the crime.

V/O: Judge Desai was involved in drafting the Victims Charter, which is a Bill of Rights for victims.

Siraj: The Victim’s Charter is in effect an attempt to give voice to the victims in determining the release of an offender on parole. You should leave your name with the parole board as a victim and ask to make representations at the appropriate time. Once you’ve done that, the Department of Correctional services or the parole board is obliged to communicate with you prior to considering the release an offender on parole.

Anjum: It’s our right to attend, our right for our voices to be heard. I would have been there.

Grace: We still believe as a department that victim representation is very important, and that is why we have taken the decision of the Parole Board for review.

Link: As things stand now these gates will open for Dr Sabadia on the 20th of June. But because the family were denied the right to be present at the hearing, the possibility exists that that decision will be reversed.

V/O: Ironically, the decision to place Sabadia on parole, may keep him behind bars even longer.

Julian: I’m just beginning to wonder whether the Parole Board didn’t do this deliberately to actually prolong his period in prison, because it’s going to be months before we have the next hearing.

V/O: But at least Zahida’s daughters will finally have their say.

Khatija: Justice also needs to be served, and he is paving the way for many other spousal killings. It’s unfair.

Anjum: One of the cardinal issues of parole is actually taking responsibility for your actions and he’s never done that. We’ve never had an apology, he has never tried to make amends with us.

Julian: I think it’s common cause that he has shown tremendous remorse in his incarceration. Whether the family will ever forgive him is another thing.

Anjum: Twenty-one years later we have not had an apology from him, or an admission, so I don’t think he’s rehabilitated.
